pr.title: match lowering: don't collect test alternatives ahead of time
pr.description:
I'm very happy with this one. Before this, when sorting candidates into the possible test branches, we manually computed `usize` indices to determine in which branch each candidate goes. To make this work we had a first pass that collected the possible alternatives we'd have to deal with, and a second pass that actually sorts the candidates.

In this PR, I replace `usize` indices with a dedicated enum. This makes `sort_candidates` easier to follow, and we don't need the first pass anymore.

r? @matthewjasper
pr.author: Nadrieril

analysis.summary: Cross-pass knowledge from a match-lowering refactor that removed the pre-collection pass for SwitchInt alternatives and replaced usize target indices with TestBranch keys. The reusable correctness point is that single-pass sorting must not accept a later constant as a SwitchInt success arm if an earlier range candidate has already been sorted into the failure branch and covers that constant. EarlyOtherwiseBranch and SimplifyCfg test-expectation changes in this PR reflect block allocation/renumbering, not a changed optimization invariant in those passes. This is based on source inspection only; no compiler execution or reproduction is claimed.
analysis.originalLogic: Before this PR, match lowering collected the possible test alternatives ahead of time: SwitchInt constants were added in one pass, and candidates were sorted afterwards using indices into that collection. In that two-pass model, if the first pass accepted a range such as `0..=5` and then a later constant `1` was added to the SwitchInt options, the second pass would no longer accept `0..=5` because `1` was already listed in those options. Thus a later constant could influence whether an earlier range was classified as failure-only.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: In the single-pass replacement, a range candidate not containing previously seen constants could be sorted into `TestBranch::Failure` before later candidates were examined. A later constant contained in that already-failure-sorted range was still accepted into `TestBranch::Constant`, adding a SwitchInt success arm that selects the later arm for a value covered by the earlier range. The incorrect transformation is accepting that constant as a success case without checking whether any already-sorted failure-branch candidate has a covering range; it is not the corrected conflict check shown in the final patch.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust `match` on an integral or `char` scrutinee lowered through `TestKind::SwitchInt`, with a range pattern occurring earlier in candidate order than a constant pattern contained in that range, where earlier constants are not in the range. The regression source is `match 1 { 10 => unreachable!(), 0..=5 => {}, 1 => unreachable!(), _ => unreachable!(), }`. Bool uses `TestKind::If`, and enums use `TestKind::Switch`, so they are outside this specific SwitchInt trigger.
analysis.trigger: A `SwitchInt` candidate list where an earlier range is sorted into the failure branch before a later constant candidate whose value is contained in that range is considered, causing the later constant to be incorrectly added as a success arm.
preconditions: The match scrutinee type is integral or `char`, so lowering chooses `TestKind::SwitchInt`.
The candidate order has a range pattern before a constant pattern that the range contains.
No earlier constant is contained in the range, so the range can initially be classified as failure-only.
Sorting proceeds from the range candidate to the later constant candidate before the constant is rejected or sorting is stopped.
pitfalls: A range already sorted into the failure branch is not safe to ignore while later success arms are discovered; the candidate set is still being formed.
Containment that is unknown (`range.contains` returns `None`) must be treated conservatively as a possible conflict, as the fix does with `None | Some(true)`.
Do not attribute this bug to `EarlyOtherwiseBranch` or `SimplifyCfg`; their changed expectations are downstream block-number/CFG-shape churn from match lowering allocating blocks differently.
The `usize`-to-`TestBranch` enum replacement is bookkeeping; the historical incorrect transformation is the single-pass ordering/acceptance of a later covered constant, not the enum itself.

The regression source intentionally allows unreachable patterns because `1` is covered by the earlier `0..=5` arm; a compile-only test is weaker than a run-pass test that would panic if the wrong arm were selected.
analysis.testStrategy: Add a focused run-pass UI regression test under integer-range match tests using the source-backed case: `match 1 { 10 => unreachable!(), 0..=5 => {}, 1 => unreachable!(), _ => unreachable!(), }` with `#![allow(unreachable_patterns)]`, so executing the match must select the range arm. Pair it with MIR inspection asserting that a constant covered by an earlier range already sorted to failure is not emitted as a SwitchInt success arm. Also exercise boundary/open integral and char ranges where `contains` can return true, false, or unknown. For `EarlyOtherwiseBranch` and `SimplifyCfg`, update expected block labels/switch arm ordering only after confirming the source-level semantics are unchanged; the historical expectation diffs show renumbered blocks such as `[0: bb2, 1: bb3]` becoming `[0: bb3, 1: bb2]`, not a new pass invariant.
